title: MoL: Adaptive Mixture-of-Length Reasoning for Efficient Question Answering with Context
claim: Our method reaches higher accuracy at far fewer tokens than baselines, dominating the accuracy-efficiency trade-off frontier.
layout: 1 panel line plot, accuracy vs log token length, ours highlighted on top-left
description: A single line chart plotting Accuracy (%) on the y-axis (50 to 70) against Token Length on a log-scaled x-axis (128, 256, 512, 1024). Five series with distinct colors and markers: Original (red squares, solid), GRPO (green triangles, dashed), EMPLP (purple diamonds, dash-dot), KIMI (yellow inverted triangles, dotted), and MoL (Ours) (blue circles, solid). A legend sits in the lower right. The blue MoL curve lies in the upper left, above all the others. It reaches about 59% accuracy at around 128 tokens and about 70% at roughly 540 tokens. The baselines sit lower and to the right. Original and GRPO extend out to about 1,100 tokens and need many more tokens to match MoL's accuracy. The eye goes first to the blue curve at the top.
caption: An evaluation of model accuracy and token length on HotpotQA: Original (base model), GRPO (RL with accuracy reward only), ERPLP (difficulty-aware adaptive reasoning depth), KIMI (length-penalized reasoning compression), and MoL (ours). Lower tokens at similar or higher accuracy is better.
abstract: We present Mixture-of-Length (MoL), an approach for Question Answering (QA) with context that aims to improve the balance between reasoning quality and response efficiency. Our method introduces a principled difficulty assessment based on information-theoretic principles and a dual-objective reward mechanism that adaptively modulates response length. In our experiments, MoL exhibits an emergent behavior termed "intelligent brevity": the model tends to produce shorter responses for simpler queries and longer ones for more complex inputs. This property is desirable for human-computer interaction and can reduce inference costs. A post-hoc analysis of internal activations suggests a correlation between this output adaptivity and the effective number of layers that contribute during inference. On multiple QA benchmarks, MoL demonstrates competitive accuracy while substantially reducing tokens compared to baselines, indicating that difficulty-aware length modulation is a promising direction for efficient QA with context.
